cards.question: List the 7 OSI layers in exact order, from Layer 7 down to Layer 1.
cards.answer:
1. Application
  2. Presentation
  3. Session
  4. Transport
  5. Network
  6. Data Link
  7. Physical
cards.explanation: Top-down mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing. Bottom-up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. The sender encapsulates from Layer 7 downward; the receiver de-encapsulates from Layer 1 upward.

cards.question: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at each layer?
cards.answer:
LayerPDU
7 ApplicationData
6 PresentationData
5 SessionData
4 TransportSegment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP)
3 NetworkPacket
2 Data LinkFrame
1 PhysicalBits
cards.explanation: Layers 5 to 7 all carry plain "Data". Only Layer 2 adds both a header and a trailer (the Frame Check Sequence). Layer 1 adds no headers; it converts bits to electrical impulses, light pulses or radio waves.

cards.question: What does each layer actually do?
cards.answer:
• 7 Application: network services for software (HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP)
  • 6 Presentation: translation, encryption, compression (SSL/TLS, JPEG, MPEG)
  • 5 Session: set up, maintain and cleanly end sessions; checkpoints (NetBIOS, PPTP; Zoom, Remote Desktop)
  • 4 Transport: end-to-end delivery, ports, flow control, reliability (TCP, UDP)
  • 3 Network: logical addressing and routing between networks (IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP; routers)
  • 2 Data Link: node-to-node delivery inside a LAN, MAC addressing, error detection (Ethernet, CSMA/CD for wired collision detection, CSMA/CA for Wi-Fi collision avoidance; NICs, switches)
  • 1 Physical: raw bit transmission over a medium (UTP, fiber, radio; hubs and MAUs, Media Access Units)
cards.explanation: Think "which question does this layer answer?" L7: what service? L6: what format? L5: which conversation? L4: which process/port and how reliably? L3: which network? L2: which local device? L1: which signal? A MAU is functionally a hub for legacy/Token Ring-style shared media; CSMA/CD lets wired Ethernet devices detect and recover from collisions, while CSMA/CA lets Wi-Fi devices avoid them up front since wireless can't reliably detect a collision while transmitting.

cards.question: What does each layer add during encapsulation?
cards.answer:
• L7: generates the raw payload from user interaction
  • L6: formats/encrypts the data
  • L5: session identifiers
  • L4: ports; TCP also adds sequence and acknowledgment numbers
  • L3: IP header with source/destination IP and TTL
  • L2: header (source/destination MAC) plus trailer (FCS)
  • L1: nothing; just signals
cards.explanation: On receipt, the NIC recomputes the FCS. If it matches, the header/trailer are stripped and the payload is passed up the stack.

cards.question: A layer-by-layer failure guide: which layer matches each symptom?
cards.answer:
SymptomLayer
Dead link, cut cable, burnt port, Wi-Fi radio off1
Cannot talk to local neighbors; switching loop storm; MAC conflicts2
LAN works but ping 8.8.8.8 fails (no default gateway / routing black hole)3
Pings work, app times out (firewall blocks TCP 443)4
Auth token expires; persistent DB connection drops5
SSL certificate error; scrambled video artifacts6
Infrastructure fine but API returns HTTP 5007
cards.explanation: Work bottom-up: confirm the link, then local delivery, then routing, then the port/service, then the application.

cards.question: Where does ARP belong in the OSI model?
cards.answer: On the boundary between Layer 2 and Layer 3, but engineers classify it as Layer 2.
cards.explanation: ARP resolves a known Layer 3 IP address into an unknown Layer 2 MAC address. Its messages are encapsulated directly in Ethernet frames and never leave the LAN, hence the Layer 2 label, even though its whole job is to serve Layer 3.

cards.question: Why is ICMP considered a Layer 3 protocol?
cards.answer: Because it is tightly integrated with IP and uses no ports, even though it is packaged inside an IP packet.
cards.explanation: An ICMP message looks like a Layer 4 payload, but it reports routing errors and congestion on behalf of IP (ping to 8.8.8.8, TTL Exceeded, Destination Unreachable), so it sits at Layer 3.

cards.question: How do Layer 4 ports map to OS sockets?
cards.answer: A port is a logical number (e.g. 80 for HTTP); a socket is the OS kernel's binding of IP address + port (e.g. 192.168.1.50:80).
cards.explanation: When a Layer 4 segment arrives, the OS reads the destination port, finds the matching socket, and hands the payload to the listening process (your web server).

cards.question: Describe the anatomy of a 48-bit MAC address.
cards.answer:
PartPositionMeaning
OUIFirst 24 bits (bytes 1-3)Vendor ID assigned by the IEEE
I/G bitLSB of byte 10 = unicast, 1 = multicast/broadcast
U/L bit2nd LSB of byte 10 = universally (factory) administered, 1 = locally administered
NIC-specificLast 24 bits (bytes 4-6)Serial number assigned by the manufacturer
cards.explanation: Written as six hex pairs, for example 15-EF-A3-45-9B-57. It is burned into the NIC, like a VIN on a car. Switches forward frames exclusively based on MAC addresses.

cards.question: The first byte of a MAC is FC. Read the I/G and U/L flags. What is the fast shortcut for spotting locally administered MACs?
cards.answer: FC = 1111 1100. Far-right bit 0 = unicast; second-from-right bit 0 = universally administered (factory).
cards.explanation: One hex digit is one nibble (4 bits). Shortcut: if the second hex digit of the MAC is 2, 6, A or E (e.g. 02-50-56...), it is locally administered, such as a spoofed MAC or a hypervisor-assigned one.

cards.question: How does a switch learn, forward and flood? What is unknown unicast flooding?
cards.answer:
1. Learn: read the source MAC, store it with the ingress port in the CAM table.
  2. Forward: read the destination MAC; if it is in the CAM table, send out only that port.
  3. Flood: if it is unknown, send out every port except the one it arrived on (unknown unicast flooding).
cards.explanation: Analogy: a mailroom clerk notes which room you walked out of when you drop off a letter. Check the table on a Cisco switch with show mac address-table.

cards.question: Collision domain vs. broadcast domain: what creates and what limits each?
cards.answer: Collision domain: hubs create one big shared domain; a modern switch gives every port its own (full-duplex removes collisions). Broadcast domain: a whole VLAN; only a Layer 3 router stops broadcasts.
cards.explanation: Switches forward broadcasts (such as ARP requests) out of all ports. That is why routers, not switches, mark the boundary between broadcast domains.

cards.question: What is MAC flapping?
cards.answer: The CAM table entry for one MAC rapidly jumps between ports because two devices on the same VLAN share the same MAC address.
cards.explanation: Typical cause: a hypervisor cloning error or misconfiguration. Frame 1 arrives on Port 2, so the MAC maps to Port 2; Frame 2 arrives on Port 8, so it is overwritten to Port 8. Result: high switch CPU and heavy packet loss because return traffic goes to the wrong port.

cards.question: How does ARP work, and what is a Gratuitous ARP (GARP) used for?
cards.answer: ARP: a host broadcasts "Who has 192.168.1.50? Tell my MAC," and the owner replies with a unicast frame containing its MAC. GARP: an unsolicited ARP reply.
cards.explanation: GARP example: an HA firewall fails over and the backup assumes the primary's IP. It broadcasts a GARP so all local switches and hosts immediately update their tables to the backup's port, minimizing downtime.

cards.question: What is ARP poisoning and how do switches defend against it?
cards.answer: An attacker sends a forged ARP reply ("I am the default gateway") so the victim caches the attacker's MAC: a man-in-the-middle attack. Defense: DHCP Snooping + Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI).
cards.explanation: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated. DHCP Snooping watches DORA transactions and builds a trusted binding table (e.g. MAC AA-AA belongs to IP .50 on Port 4). DAI checks every ARP packet against it and drops mismatches in hardware. Cryptography was not added to ARP because per-resolution hashing would add unacceptable CPU overhead and latency.

cards.question: Explain the key IPv4 header fields: TTL, Protocol, fragmentation fields and Header Checksum.
cards.answer:
• TTL (8 bits): decremented at every router; at 0 the packet is dropped and ICMP Time Exceeded is sent.
  • Protocol (8 bits): TCP = 6, UDP = 17, ICMP = 1.
  • Identification / Flags (DF, MF) / Fragment Offset: group, control and order fragments when a packet exceeds the MTU (1500 bytes on Ethernet).
  • Header Checksum: integrity of the IP header.
cards.explanation: The header is a 20-byte control structure (minimum). Because TTL changes at every hop, every router must recalculate and rewrite the checksum.

cards.question: Classful vs. CIDR: what changed and what does /24 mean?
cards.answer: Classful: Class A 10.0.0.0/8, Class B 172.16.0.0/16, Class C 192.168.0.0/24 (fixed boundaries). CIDR removes fixed boundaries; /24 means the first 24 bits are the network portion.
cards.explanation: Classful routing wasted millions of addresses. Every address is a Network ID (street) plus a Host ID (house). The private Class C range 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 is for LANs and needs NAT to reach the Internet.

cards.question: Define the four identifiers of every subnet: mask, Network ID, Broadcast ID and usable host range.
cards.answer:
• Subnet mask: 32-bit rulebook; 1s = network bits, 0s = host bits. Routers apply a bitwise AND with the destination IP.
  • Network ID: lowest address (host bits all 0); identifies the subnet; not assignable.
  • Broadcast ID: highest address (host bits all 1); reaches all hosts; not assignable.
  • Usable range: everything between; count = 2h − 2 (h = host bits).
cards.explanation: Example: 192.168.1.0/24 has Network ID .0, Broadcast .255, usable .1 to .254 (254 hosts).

cards.question: Why do you almost always see 255.255.255.0 on your own PC?
cards.answer: It is the default (/24) for consumer routers and standard office networks: 254 usable hosts.
cards.explanation: Plenty of room for laptops and phones, yet small enough that broadcast traffic will not overwhelm devices. Enterprises customize with VLSM (e.g. 255.255.255.252 for a router-to-router link, avoiding 252 wasted addresses).

cards.question: VLSM walkthrough: carve 192.168.4.0/24 into 60-host (Front Desk), 25-host (Storage) and 2-host (WAN link) subnets.
cards.answer:
SubnetHost bitsCIDR / MaskNetwork IDUsable rangeBroadcast
Front Desk (60)6 (62 usable)/26 255.255.255.192192.168.4.0.1 to .62.63
Storage (25)5 (30 usable)/27 255.255.255.224192.168.4.64.65 to .94.95
WAN link (2)2 (2 usable)/30 255.255.255.252192.168.4.96.97 to .98.99
cards.explanation:
Rule: carve from the largest requirement to the smallest, and start each new Network ID immediately after the previous Broadcast ID. A /27 is 32 addresses, so 64 + 32 = 96 is the next free boundary.
Reviewer correction: the PDF's Storage row shows .65-.126 and broadcast .127; those are /26 numbers. A /27 starting at .64 ends at .95 (30 hosts).

cards.question: Why does a /31 mask work on point-to-point links (RFC 3021)?
cards.answer: A /31 leaves 1 host bit (two addresses). On a link with exactly two devices, no broadcast is needed, so both addresses (.0 and .1) are assigned to the router interfaces.
cards.explanation: Traditional rules reserve the Network and Broadcast IDs, which would leave zero usable hosts. RFC 3021 changed the OS logic for point-to-point links, disabling broadcast behavior and saving huge numbers of addresses across ISP backbones.

cards.question: IPv6 core architecture: structure, shorthand rules, SLAAC and the end of broadcast.
cards.answer:
• 128 bits = 8 hextets of 16 bits, e.g. 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
  • Drop leading zeros in a hextet; replace one run of all-zero hextets with :: (only once): 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334
  • Subnets are standardized at /64 for SLAAC.
  • No broadcast: unicast, anycast and targeted multicast only.
cards.explanation: SLAAC (EUI-64): split the 48-bit MAC in half, insert FFFE in the middle (24 + 16 + 24 = 64 bits) and flip the U/L bit. The device builds its own unique Host ID without DHCP. IPv6 restores end-to-end routing without NAT.

cards.question: A packet exceeds the path MTU and the Don't Fragment (DF) bit is 1. What happens?
cards.answer: The router drops it and sends back ICMP Type 3, Code 4 ("Fragmentation Needed and DF Set") containing the egress MTU. This is Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD).
cards.explanation: Steps: (1) hardware detects the MTU mismatch and drops the packet; (2) the router CPU generates the ICMP message; (3) it inserts the exact MTU (e.g. 1400); (4) the source shrinks its TCP Maximum Segment Size for that session.

cards.question: Compare copper categories: speed, frequency and maximum distance.
cards.answer:
CategorySpeedFrequencyDistance
Cat5e1 Gbps100 MHz100 m
Cat610 Gbps250 MHz55 m at 10G (100 m at 1G)
Cat6a10 Gbps500 MHz100 m
Cat710 Gbps600 MHz100 m
Cat840 Gbps2000 MHz30 m
cards.explanation: Standard Ethernet copper is limited to 100 m (328 ft) per channel. Cat6 uses a plastic spline to cut crosstalk; Cat6a has thicker insulation and tighter twists; Cat7 needs shielding on every pair; Cat8 is for short data-center switch-to-server links.

cards.question: UTP vs. STP: how does each fight interference, and what is the STP grounding requirement?
cards.answer: UTP relies on tightly twisted pairs whose opposing fields cancel (destructive interference). STP adds foil or braided shielding and must be grounded at the patch panel.
cards.explanation: Copper acts as an antenna for EMI (fluorescent lights, motors, adjacent cables: alien crosstalk). Without a ground, an STP shield traps ambient EMI and destroys data integrity.

cards.question: T568A vs. T568B pinouts, straight-through vs. crossover cables, Auto-MDIX and termination tools.
cards.answer:
Pin12345678
T568AW/GreenGreenW/OrangeBlueW/BlueOrangeW/BrownBrown
T568BW/OrangeOrangeW/GreenBlueW/BlueGreenW/BrownBrown
  • Straight-through (B to B): different devices, e.g. switch to PC.
  • Crossover (A to B): like devices, e.g. switch to switch.
cards.explanation: Modern switches use Auto-MDIX to detect the transmit pins and flip Tx/Rx automatically, making crossovers largely obsolete. Tools: wire stripper (removes the jacket), crimping tool (secures the RJ-45), punch-down tool (seats wires in patch panels/keystones).

cards.question: Single-mode vs. multi-mode fiber.
cards.answer:
Multi-mode (MMF)Single-mode (SMF)
Core50 or 62.5 microns~9 microns
Light sourceLED or VCSELHigh-powered laser
Modal dispersionHighZero
Use / reachShort-haul LAN, roughly 300 to 550 mLong-haul WAN, 10 to 100+ km
cards.explanation: In MMF, light rays take different angles (modes) and arrive at different times, smearing the signal. SMF's narrow core allows one direct path. Fiber is 100% immune to EMI.

cards.question: Name the common physical-layer pitfalls and their symptoms.
cards.answer:
• Attenuation: run over 100 m; signal falls below the NIC's threshold; dead link or heavy loss.
  • Near-End Crosstalk (NEXT): pairs untwisted too far at a keystone; signal reflections, high CRC errors.
  • Duplex mismatch: one side full, the other half; CLI shows skyrocketing late collisions.
cards.explanation: When Layer 1 fails silently you see intermittent drops, crippling latency and CRC errors on switch interfaces.

cards.question: Compare how a Layer 2 switch and a Layer 3 router operate.
cards.answer:
Switch (L2)Router (L3)
AddressesMAC (physical)IP (logical)
ScopeSame LAN subnetBetween subnets and the Internet
Decision tableCAM tableRouting table
BroadcastsForwards out all portsBlocks them (domain boundary)
cards.explanation: A switch is an office mailroom (cubicle to cubicle). A router is a city-to-city postal center: it strips the L2 frame, reads the destination IP, consults its routing table and picks the next hop.

cards.question: Why does a host need a Default Gateway?
cards.answer: The switch is a "flat" Layer 2 environment. A host ANDs the destination with its mask, sees 8.8.8.8 is off-subnet, and must send it to the gateway (e.g. 192.168.1.1), its exit door.
cards.explanation: The PC cannot broadcast a MAC request for Google because routers block broadcasts, so it ARPs for the gateway's MAC instead.

cards.question: Walk through the end-to-end journey of a ping from 192.168.1.50 to 8.8.8.8.
cards.answer:
1. PC decides 8.8.8.8 is external and targets the default gateway.
  2. ARP for the gateway (192.168.1.1) if not cached; router replies with its MAC.
  3. PC sends frame: L2 dst = router MAC; L3 src 192.168.1.50, dst 8.8.8.8.
  4. Router sees its own MAC and strips the L2 header/trailer.
  5. Routing table (or 0.0.0.0/0) chooses the WAN next hop; TTL 64 becomes 63.
  6. Router builds a new frame (src = router WAN MAC, dst = ISP router MAC). IPs untouched.
cards.explanation: L3 IPs never change (excluding NAT); L2 MACs are stripped and rewritten at every router hop until the packet reaches Google's server.

cards.question: What are NAT and PAT, and how does the state table work?
cards.answer: Private (RFC 1918) addresses are not routable on the Internet. The edge router replaces the private source IP with its public IP and tracks connections by Layer 4 source port (PAT / NAT overload).
cards.explanation: Outbound: 192.168.1.50 becomes 203.0.113.5 and the router records "port 55555 belongs to 192.168.1.50." Inbound: the reply to 203.0.113.5:55555 is matched in the state table, the destination IP is rewritten back to the private IP, and it is forwarded to the LAN. One public IP serves all 254 LAN devices.

cards.question: Do 802.1Q VLAN tags and 802.1p CoS survive a routed hop? How does QoS survive a WAN?
cards.answer: No. They live in the Ethernet header, which the router strips. The ingress router must map CoS to the IP header's DSCP field.
cards.explanation: The IP header remains intact across hops, so downstream routers read DSCP and apply their own local Layer 2 queuing priorities.

cards.question: How does a router decide whether a packet is for its Control Plane or Data Plane?
cards.answer: Data plane: destination is a remote network; the ASIC does a FIB lookup, rewrites the MAC headers, and forwards at wire speed with no CPU. Control plane: destination is one of the router's own interface IPs (or a multicast like OSPF 224.0.0.5); the ASIC punts it to the CPU.
cards.explanation: Example: an SSH session to the router is control plane; a packet transiting to 8.8.8.8 is data plane.

cards.question: Why does IP need a TTL when routing protocols already prevent loops?
cards.answer: They protect different planes. Loop-prevention (Split Horizon, Poison Reverse, AS-Path) protects the control plane; TTL is the data plane fail-safe fuse.
cards.explanation: Convergence delays, transient states or static-route mistakes can still create a real loop. TTL decrements to 0 and kills the packet, preventing a storm that would melt the links.

cards.question: Explain the DORA process with layer details.
cards.answer:
StepL2L3UDP
DiscoverClient MAC to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.25568 to 67
OfferServer MAC to Client MAC (or broadcast)Server IP to 255.255.255.25567 to 68
RequestClient MAC to broadcast0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.25568 to 67
AcknowledgeServer MAC to Client MACServer IP to 255.255.255.25567 to 68
cards.explanation: The client has no IP, so it relies on L2 MACs and L3 broadcasts. The Request is broadcast so the winning server hears "I accept" and losing servers return their offers to the pool. The proposed IP travels inside the DHCP payload; the OS validates it before binding it to the interface.

cards.question: Static vs. DHCP addressing, and what is APIPA?
cards.answer: Static: routers, switches, servers, printers (must never change). DHCP: laptops, phones, tablets (transient). APIPA: if no DHCP server answers, the OS self-assigns 169.254.x.x.
cards.explanation: "Obtain an IP address automatically" in Windows means DHCP. APIPA allows local-link communication only; it is not routable across the Internet.

cards.question: How does a DHCP Relay Agent (ip helper-address) let clients reach a server on another subnet?
cards.answer: Routers drop broadcasts, so the router converts the client's UDP 67 broadcast into a unicast to the central DHCP server and inserts its client-facing interface IP in the giaddr field.
cards.explanation:
Configure it on the interface facing the clients, not the server. The server reads giaddr to pick the right pool and returns a unicast Offer via the router.
R1(config)# interface gigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.0.99.5

cards.question: What are the T1 and T2 lease timers?
cards.answer: T1 (50%): unicast DHCP Request to the original server to renew. T2 (87.5%): if that fails, broadcast a DHCP Request to any server (rebinding). At 100% the client must surrender the IP.
cards.explanation: These hidden timers ensure the client never unexpectedly loses its IP while the original server is up, and give it a second chance when the server is down.

cards.question: Configure a Cisco router as a DHCP server. What is the order of operations?
cards.answer:
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.20
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool VLAN10_USERS
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# dns-server 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
R1(dhcp-config)# domain-name corp.local
cards.explanation: Exclude addresses before creating the pool (gateway, switches, servers, printers) or the router may lease an address already in use. The router matches the ingress interface's subnet to the pool's network statement. Benefit: no single point of failure; a branch keeps handing out IPs if the WAN drops.

cards.question: Which commands verify and troubleshoot DHCP on a Cisco router?
cards.answer:
• show ip dhcp binding: leased IP to MAC mapping with expiry
  • show ip dhcp pool: total, leased and excluded addresses (scope exhaustion)
  • show ip dhcp conflict: IPs the router found already in use
  • clear ip dhcp binding * / clear ip dhcp conflict *
  • debug ip dhcp server events: live DORA logging
cards.explanation: Before offering an IP, the router pings it. If something replies, a rogue device is using it, so the address is flagged as a conflict and not leased.

cards.question: What are the Cisco IOS navigation modes and how do you enter each?
cards.answer:
ModePromptEnter with
User EXECRouter>Default entry point
Privileged EXECRouter#enable
Global ConfigurationRouter(config)#configure terminal
InterfaceRouter(config-if)#interface g0/0/0

cards.explanation: User EXEC is "look but don't touch" (ping, limited show). Privileged EXEC is the admin view (all show, debug, file commands, but no config changes). Global config affects the whole device. Interface mode applies IP, speed and duplex to one interface. Line mode configures console/VTY access.

cards.question: What is the command to save the configuration to NVRAM?
cards.answer: copy running-config startup-config (short: copy run start) or the legacy write memory (wr), from Privileged EXEC mode.
cards.explanation: RAM is volatile: without saving, a reboot wipes the running configuration. The startup configuration lives in NVRAM.

cards.question: Why does the first ping to a new gateway/destination time out while the next three succeed?
cards.answer: The first echo request is lost while ARP resolves the destination MAC. Once the MAC is cached, pings 2, 3 and 4 succeed.
cards.explanation: 1) The PC generates an ICMP Echo Request. 2) Its ARP cache is empty. 3) It broadcasts an ARP request. 4) The reply returns and the MAC is cached. 5) Meanwhile the ping timeout (about 2 s) expires: "Request timed out." Cisco IOS devices show the same effect as .!!!! (first ping fails, the rest succeed). Verify with arp -a.

cards.question: Packet Tracer vs. GNS3/EVE-NG/CML: simulation or emulation?
cards.answer: Packet Tracer is a simulator (it mimics protocol behavior and does not run real IOS). GNS3, EVE-NG and Cisco CML are emulators that boot real IOS binaries via hypervisors such as QEMU.
cards.explanation: Packet Tracer is perfect for CCNA-level work but cannot replicate obscure bugs, advanced BGP edge cases or hardware quirks.

cards.question: Realtime mode vs. Simulation mode in Packet Tracer?
cards.answer: Realtime: the network runs dynamically as in production. Simulation: a turn-based debugger that pauses time and intercepts every PDU.
cards.explanation: Click a paused packet's envelope to see Inbound/Outbound PDU Details across the OSI layers: watch the router strip the inbound L2 header and rewrite the outbound one while the L3 IPs stay untouched.

cards.question: What are the essential IOS CLI shortcuts (?, Tab, do)?
cards.answer:
• ? lists options: ip ? shows what can follow ip; int? lists commands starting with "int".
  • Tab completes a command (conf becomes configure).
  • do runs Privileged EXEC commands from a sub-mode: do show ip route.
cards.explanation: Normally show commands only work at the # prompt; do saves you from backing out of config mode.

cards.question: Build and harden the basic topology: what is the cabling and the router baseline configuration?
cards.answer:
Devices: a PC, a Cisco Catalyst 2960 switch and a Cisco 4321 router. Cabling: PC to switch (straight-through), switch to router's GigabitEthernet port (straight-through).
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1-Core
R1-Core(config)# enable secret Cisco123!
R1-Core(config)# line con 0
R1-Core(config-line)# password ConsolePass
R1-Core(config-line)# login
R1-Core(config-line)# exit
R1-Core(config)# service password-encryption
R1-Core(config)# banner motd # UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS PROHIBITED #
R1-Core(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/0/0
R1-Core(config-if)# description Link-to-LAN-Switch
R1-Core(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1-Core(config-if)# no shutdown
cards.explanation:
login forces the console to prompt for the password. no shutdown brings the interface (Layer 1 state) up.
Exam nuance: enable secret stores a hash, while service password-encryption applies only weak, reversible Type 7 encryption to plaintext passwords.

cards.question: Two hosts on the same switch, A = 192.168.1.10/24 and B = 192.168.1.130/25. What goes wrong?
cards.answer: They disagree about what is on-link. A thinks B is local and sends directly; B thinks A is off-subnet and sends its replies to its default gateway (or has nowhere to send them).
cards.explanation:
A's /24 covers .0 to .255, so B (.130) looks local and A ARPs for it. B's /25 covers .128 to .255, so A (.10) looks remote. ARP itself still works, because an ARP reply is unicast to the requester's MAC and does not consult the mask. The breakage is asymmetric Layer 3 return traffic that fails the TCP handshake.
Reviewer correction: the PDF says B sends its ARP reply to the gateway. It does not; the mismatch bites at Layer 3, on B's return traffic.

cards.question: What happens if a host's Default Gateway IP belongs to an ordinary PC on the same subnet?
cards.answer: The host ARPs for that IP, the PC replies with its MAC, and frames reach it, but the PC silently drops them because IP forwarding is off: a black hole.
cards.explanation: The PC's NIC accepts the frame (L2 MAC matches). The OS then sees the L3 destination is not itself and, having no routing enabled in its kernel, discards the packet.

cards.question: How does a switch avoid broadcast storms from cabling loops before STP converges?
cards.answer: Managed switches put ports in Blocking/Listening when a link comes up: BPDUs pass, but user data and broadcasts are dropped until the topology is proven loop-free.
cards.explanation: Classic STP takes roughly 30 to 50 seconds; Rapid STP about 2 seconds. An unmanaged switch has no STP, so a loop makes broadcasts circulate and multiply until buffers overflow and the CPU locks up.

cards.question: What is TCP "Zero Windowing"?
cards.answer: The receiver advertises Window Size = 0 in its ACK because its buffer is full; the sender halts transmission.
cards.explanation: This is flow control protecting a slow client from a fast server (e.g. Gigabit server, 10 Mbps client). The sender periodically sends 1-byte Zero Window Probes; when the client drains its backlog it advertises a non-zero window and transmission resumes.

questions.question: Which layer routes packets between different networks?
questions.explanation: Layer 3 uses logical IP addressing; routers compare the destination IP to a routing table to choose the next hop. Layer 2 only moves frames inside one LAN.

questions.question: What is the PDU at the Data Link layer?
questions.explanation: L1 = Bits, L2 = Frame, L3 = Packet, L4 = Segment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP), L5 to L7 = Data.

questions.question: Type the PDU name for UDP at Layer 4.
questions.explanation: TCP produces segments; UDP produces datagrams.

questions.question: Which layer adds both a header and a trailer (FCS) during encapsulation?
questions.explanation: The L2 header holds source/destination MACs; the trailer carries the Frame Check Sequence for error detection. Layer 1 adds nothing.

questions.question: SSL/TLS, JPEG and MPEG belong to which layer?
questions.explanation: The Presentation layer handles translation, encryption and compression.

questions.question: NetBIOS, PPTP, and managing a Zoom or Remote Desktop session are associated with which layer?
questions.explanation: The Session layer establishes, maintains and cleanly terminates sessions and can restart from checkpoints.

questions.question: You can reach devices on your Wi-Fi but ping 8.8.8.8 fails. What is the most likely problem?
options: Layer 3: missing default gateway or routing black hole
questions.explanation: Local traffic works (L1/L2 fine) but nothing leaves the subnet, so suspect the gateway or routing.

questions.question: Pings succeed, but an application times out because a firewall blocks TCP 443. Which layer is at fault?
questions.explanation: Reachability (L3) is fine; port-based filtering happens at Layer 4.

questions.question: Data arrives intact but the browser shows an SSL certificate error. Which layer is implicated?
questions.explanation: TLS negotiation and encryption are presentation-layer functions in this model.

questions.question: Why is ICMP placed at Layer 3 even though it rides inside an IP packet?
options: It uses no ports and is integrated with IP to report routing errors
It is carried directly in Ethernet frames
questions.explanation: ICMP has no port numbers, so it does not behave like a Layer 4 protocol; it reports errors and congestion on behalf of IP.

questions.question: ARP messages ride directly inside Ethernet frames and never leave the LAN. Where do engineers classify ARP?
options: Layer 2 (serving Layer 3, on the L2/L3 boundary)
questions.explanation: ARP resolves a known IP (L3) into an unknown MAC (L2). Because it is encapsulated directly in Ethernet, it is treated as Layer 2.

questions.question: A "socket" is best defined as:
options: The OS binding of an IP address plus a port number (e.g. 192.168.1.50:80)
The RJ-45 jack on a NIC
questions.explanation: On arrival, the OS reads the destination port, finds the matching socket and hands the payload to the listening process.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a Layer 2 media access protocol to its medium?
options: CSMA/CD for wired Ethernet collision detection, CSMA/CA for Wi-Fi collision avoidance
CSMA/CA for wired Ethernet, CSMA/CD for Wi-Fi
CSMA/CD for both wired and wireless
questions.explanation: Wired NICs can sense a collision while transmitting (CD); Wi-Fi radios generally cannot, so they avoid collisions in advance (CA) instead.

questions.question: True or False: Only the Data Link layer's encapsulation adds both a header and a trailer.
questions.explanation: Layer 2 adds a header (source/destination MAC) plus a trailer (the Frame Check Sequence). Every other layer that adds anything only adds a header.

questions.question: True or False: The Protocol Data Unit for Layers 5, 6, and 7 is called a Segment.
questions.explanation: Layers 5 to 7 all carry plain "Data." Segment is the Layer 4 PDU for TCP specifically (UDP uses Datagram).

questions.question: True or False: ICMP messages use TCP or UDP port numbers, just like other transport-layer traffic.
questions.explanation: ICMP uses no ports at all. That is exactly why, even though it rides inside an IP packet, it is classified as a Layer 3 protocol rather than Layer 4.

questions.question: Match each OSI layer to its Protocol Data Unit (PDU).
questions.explanation: Layers 5 to 7 all use the generic PDU name "Data." Only Layer 4 has two names depending on protocol: Segment for TCP, Datagram for UDP.

questions.question: How long is an IEEE 802 MAC address?
questions.explanation: Six hexadecimal pairs, e.g. 15-EF-A3-45-9B-57.

questions.question: What is the OUI in a MAC address?
options: The first 24 bits, assigned by the IEEE to the manufacturer
The last 24 bits, a device serial number
questions.explanation: OUI = bytes 1 to 3 (vendor). The last 24 bits are the NIC-specific ID.

questions.question: The first byte of a MAC is FC (1111 1100). What do the I/G and U/L bits indicate?
questions.explanation: I/G is the least significant bit (0 = unicast). U/L is the second least significant bit (0 = burned-in/universal).

questions.question: Which MAC address is locally administered (e.g. assigned by a hypervisor)?
questions.explanation: 0x02 = 0000 0010, so the U/L bit is 1. Shortcut: a second hex digit of 2, 6, A or E means locally administered.

questions.question: A switch builds its CAM table by reading the:
questions.explanation: It records the source MAC with the ingress port. The destination MAC is used for the forwarding lookup.

questions.question: The destination MAC is not in the CAM table. The switch:
options: Floods the frame out all ports except the ingress port
Sends it only out the uplink
questions.explanation: This is unknown unicast flooding.

questions.question: Type the Cisco IOS command that displays a switch's MAC address (CAM) table.
questions.explanation: It lists MAC, VLAN, type and port. show mac address-table is current syntax; older IOS used show mac-address-table.

questions.question: How many collision domains does a modern full-duplex switch create?
options: None; collisions still happen on every port
questions.explanation: Hubs create one shared collision domain; switches isolate every port.

questions.question: A VLAN represents one ______ domain (fill in the blank).
questions.explanation: Switches flood broadcasts within a VLAN; only a Layer 3 router stops them.

questions.question: The same MAC keeps appearing on Port 2, then Port 8, then Port 2 again. What is this and what causes it?
options: MAC flapping: duplicate MACs (e.g. a cloned VM) on one VLAN
Unknown unicast flooding: a full CAM table
questions.explanation: Each frame overwrites the CAM entry, spiking switch CPU and sending return traffic to the wrong port.

questions.question: An ARP request is sent as:
options: A unicast to the default gateway
questions.explanation: "Who has 192.168.1.50? Tell my MAC." The owner replies with a unicast frame.

questions.question: Why does an HA firewall send a Gratuitous ARP after failover?
options: To make switches and hosts immediately update their tables to the new unit's port and MAC
questions.explanation: The backup assumes the primary's IP and announces it so CAM and ARP entries update immediately.

questions.question: An attacker sends a forged ARP reply saying "I am the default gateway." This is:
options: ARP poisoning enabling a man-in-the-middle attack
questions.explanation: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated, so the victim caches the attacker's MAC for the gateway IP.

questions.question: Which pair of switch features mitigates ARP spoofing?
options: DHCP Snooping plus Dynamic ARP Inspection
questions.explanation: Snooping builds a trusted IP-MAC-port binding table; DAI drops ARP packets that contradict it.

questions.question: True or False: A MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes) long.
questions.explanation: Written as six hexadecimal pairs, e.g. 15-EF-A3-45-9B-57: 3 bytes of OUI plus 3 bytes of NIC-specific serial number.

questions.question: True or False: When a frame's destination MAC is already in the CAM table, the switch floods it out every port.
questions.explanation: That describes unknown unicast flooding, used only when the destination MAC is NOT in the table. A known MAC is forwarded out just the one recorded port.

questions.question: Match each part of a 48-bit MAC address to what it represents.
pairs: Vendor ID assigned by the IEEE
Unique serial number set by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: I/G is the least significant bit of the first byte; U/L is the second-least significant bit. A second hex digit of 2, 6, A or E signals a locally administered (e.g. spoofed or hypervisor-assigned) MAC.

questions.question: What does a router do to the IP TTL at each hop?
options: Decrements it by 1; at 0 the packet is dropped and ICMP Time Exceeded is sent
questions.explanation: TTL is an 8-bit anti-loop fuse.

questions.question: Which set of IPv4 Protocol field values is correct?
questions.explanation: The 8-bit Protocol field tells the receiver which upper-layer process gets the payload.

questions.question: Why must every router recalculate the IPv4 Header Checksum?
options: The TTL changes at each hop
questions.explanation: Any change to the header invalidates the old checksum.

questions.question: Which IPv4 field groups fragments that belong to the same original packet?
questions.explanation: Identification groups fragments; Flags carry DF/MF; Fragment Offset gives the reassembly order.

questions.question: What is the typical Ethernet MTU, in bytes?
questions.explanation: Packets larger than the link MTU are fragmented (or dropped if DF = 1).

questions.question: A router finds the network portion of a destination by:
options: A bitwise AND of the IP address and the subnet mask
A bitwise OR of the IP address and the mask
An XOR of the IP address and the MAC
questions.explanation: Where the mask has 1s the network bits are kept; 0s are host bits.

questions.question: Which of these is not a valid IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: The double colon may appear only once; otherwise the number of zero hextets is ambiguous.

questions.question: What is the standard IPv6 subnet prefix length required for SLAAC?
questions.explanation: 64 network bits plus a 64-bit Interface ID.

questions.question: How is an EUI-64 Interface ID built from a 48-bit MAC?
options: Split the MAC in half, insert FFFE, flip the U/L bit
questions.explanation: 24 + 16 (FFFE) + 24 = 64 bits, with the U/L bit inverted.

questions.question: How does IPv6 replace IPv4 broadcast?
questions.explanation: IPv6 has no broadcast; multicast groups let only relevant hosts process discovery traffic.

questions.question: In CIDR notation, what does /24 mean?
options: The first 24 bits are the network portion

questions.question: Which private range does the module identify as the Class C private block?
questions.explanation: Private addresses are for internal LANs and are not routable on the Internet without NAT.

questions.question: True or False: Private IP addresses like 192.168.x.x are directly routable on the public Internet without NAT.
questions.explanation: RFC 1918 private addresses are strictly for internal LAN use. An ISP router receiving a packet with a private source IP drops it instantly, which is why NAT/PAT exists.

questions.question: With h host bits, the number of usable hosts is:
questions.explanation: Subtract the Network ID and the Broadcast ID.

questions.question: Which statement about a subnet's Network ID and Broadcast ID is correct?
options: Network ID = host bits all 0; Broadcast ID = host bits all 1; neither can be assigned to a host
Network ID = host bits all 1; Broadcast ID = host bits all 0
Both can be assigned to hosts
Network ID is the default gateway
questions.explanation: They are the lowest and highest addresses in the block and are reserved.

questions.question: How many usable hosts are in 192.168.1.0/24?
In VLSM, in which order should you carve subnets?
questions.explanation: Carving big blocks first keeps every block aligned on its boundary and avoids overlaps.

questions.question: A Front Desk needs 60 hosts. What is the best prefix?
questions.explanation: 60 hosts need 6 host bits (2<sup>6</sup> − 2 = 62), so 32 − 6 = /26.

questions.question: What is the traditional minimum prefix that gives 2 usable hosts for a point-to-point WAN link?
questions.explanation: 2 host bits give 4 addresses, minus Network and Broadcast = 2 usable.

questions.question: What is the dotted-decimal mask for /27?
questions.explanation: 27 network bits leave 5 host bits: 256 − 32 = 224.

questions.question: What is the dotted-decimal mask for /26?
What is the dotted-decimal mask for /28?
How many usable hosts are in a /28?
questions.explanation: 4 host bits: 2<sup>4</sup> − 2 = 14.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.4.96/28?
questions.explanation: A /28 block is 16 addresses: .96 to .111. Network ID .96, usable .97 to .110, broadcast .111.

questions.question: Storage (25 hosts) is placed at 192.168.4.64 after a /26 at .0. Which allocation is correct?
questions.explanation: 25 hosts need 5 host bits (30 usable) = /27 = 32 addresses: .64 to .95. The .126/.127 values belong to a /26.

questions.question: After 192.168.4.0/26 and 192.168.4.64/27, where does the next free block start for a /30 WAN link?
questions.explanation: The next Network ID starts right after the previous broadcast (.95). Starting at .128 is legal but leaves an unused gap.

questions.question: Why does a /31 work on a router-to-router link (RFC 3021)?
options: Only two devices exist, so no Network/Broadcast address is reserved and both addresses are assigned
It has two usable addresses plus a Network and Broadcast ID
Routers ignore masks on serial links
questions.explanation: Broadcast is meaningless on a two-node link, so the OS disables it.

questions.question: Why do you usually see 255.255.255.0 on your own PC?
options: It is the default for consumer routers and office LANs: 254 usable hosts and a manageable broadcast domain
questions.explanation: Enterprises use custom masks (VLSM) to avoid waste.

questions.question: A router-to-router link uses a default /24. How many addresses are wasted (usable but unused)?
questions.explanation: 254 usable minus the 2 needed = 252.

questions.question: True or False: A /31 subnet mask is valid on a point-to-point router link under RFC 3021.
questions.explanation: A /31 leaves only 1 host bit (2 addresses). RFC 3021 disables broadcast logic for two-device serial links so both .0 and .1 can be assigned as usable router interfaces.

questions.question: Match each CIDR prefix to its dotted-decimal subnet mask.
questions.explanation: Each step doubles the number of network bits' worth of blocks: /24 has 256 addresses per block, /26 has 64, /27 has 32, /30 has 4.

questions.question: What is the maximum length of an Ethernet copper channel?
questions.explanation: Beyond 100 m, attenuation degrades the signal.

questions.question: What is Cat6's maximum distance at 10 Gbps?
questions.explanation: Cat6 reaches 100 m only at 1 Gbps.

questions.question: Which category delivers 10 Gbps over the full 100 m (500 MHz)?
questions.explanation: Cat6a has thicker insulation and tighter twists.

questions.question: Cat8 is used for:
questions.explanation: Cat8 is heavily shielded and specialized: 2000 MHz, 30 m.

questions.question: UTP reduces crosstalk mainly by:
options: Tightly twisted pairs whose opposing fields cancel out
questions.explanation: Destructive interference between twisted transmit and receive wires; higher categories twist more per inch.

questions.question: Why must STP cabling be grounded at the patch panel?
options: Without a ground, the shield acts as an antenna that traps EMI
questions.explanation: An ungrounded shield collects ambient EMI and destroys data integrity.

questions.question: Pins 1 and 2 of T568B are:
questions.explanation: T568A starts with White/Green, Green.

questions.question: Which cable has T568A on one end and T568B on the other?
questions.explanation: Crossovers connect like devices; Auto-MDIX makes them largely obsolete.

questions.question: Which tool seats wires into a patch panel or keystone jack?
questions.explanation: A crimper secures the RJ-45 connector; the stripper removes the jacket.

questions.question: What is the core diameter of single-mode fiber?
questions.explanation: The narrow core allows a single light path: zero modal dispersion.

questions.question: Why does multi-mode fiber have a shorter reach than single-mode?
options: Modal dispersion smears the signal over distance
questions.explanation: Light rays at different angles arrive at different times.

questions.question: A switch port is hard-coded to full duplex but the endpoint fell back to half duplex. What does the CLI show?
questions.explanation: The full-duplex side transmits while the half-duplex side is transmitting, causing logical collisions.

questions.question: Intermittent drops and high CRC errors appear after pairs were untwisted too far at a keystone jack. This is:
questions.explanation: Untwisting changes impedance and causes signal reflections.

questions.question: A copper run exceeds 100 m. Which pitfall results?
questions.explanation: Signal voltage falls below the NIC's detection threshold: dead link or heavy loss.

questions.question: True or False: Standard Ethernet over copper is limited to 100 meters per channel.
questions.explanation: Beyond 100 m (328 ft), signal attenuation drops the voltage below the NIC's detection threshold.

questions.question: True or False: Multi-mode fiber has zero modal dispersion, giving it the longest reach.
questions.explanation: It is the opposite: single-mode fiber's narrow ~9-micron core gives zero modal dispersion and long-haul reach. Multi-mode has high modal dispersion, which limits it to short-haul LAN runs.

questions.question: Type the two-word tool used to remove a cable's outer jacket without nicking the copper conductors.
questions.explanation: A wire stripper removes the jacket cleanly; the crimping tool then secures the RJ-45 connector, and a punch-down tool seats wires into a patch panel or keystone jack.

questions.question: Match each copper category to its top speed and maximum reach.
questions.explanation: Cat6 needs a plastic spline to cut crosstalk but still falls back to 55 m at 10 Gbps; Cat6a's thicker insulation and tighter twists let it hold 10 Gbps for the full 100 m; Cat8 is a short, heavily shielded data-center standard.

questions.question: A PC pings 8.8.8.8. What is the destination MAC of the first frame?
questions.explanation: The frame goes to the gateway; only the IP destination is 8.8.8.8.

questions.question: Ignoring NAT, what stays unchanged end to end?
questions.explanation: L2 headers are stripped and rewritten at every router hop.

questions.question: A packet leaves the host with TTL 64. After the first router it has TTL ___.
questions.explanation: Each router decrements TTL by 1.

questions.question: What is the notation of the default route?
questions.explanation: It matches everything and is used when no more specific route exists.

questions.question: Why is NAT/PAT required for 192.168.1.50 to reach the Internet?
options: RFC 1918 private addresses are not routable on the public Internet
questions.explanation: An ISP router drops packets with a private source IP.

questions.question: How does PAT match an inbound reply to the correct LAN host?
options: Layer 4 ports recorded in a NAT state table
questions.explanation: E.g. "port 55555 belongs to 192.168.1.50."

questions.question: Which device forms the boundary of a broadcast domain?
questions.explanation: Routers block broadcasts.

questions.question: Which pairing of device and core table is correct?
options: Switch: CAM table; Router: routing table
Switch: routing table; Router: CAM table
questions.explanation: The CAM table maps MACs to ports; the routing table maps destination networks to next hops.

questions.question: Why can't a PC just broadcast a MAC request for 8.8.8.8?
options: It is off-subnet and routers block broadcasts, so the PC ARPs for the default gateway
questions.explanation: The bitwise AND with the mask shows the destination is remote, so the gateway is used.

questions.question: True or False: Across a multi-hop path (ignoring NAT), the Layer 3 IP addresses stay the same end to end while the Layer 2 MAC addresses are stripped and rewritten at every router hop.
questions.explanation: Each router deletes the inbound L2 frame, makes its routing decision from the untouched L3 IPs, and builds a brand-new L2 frame for the next hop.

questions.question: DORA stands for Discover, Offer, ______, Acknowledge.
questions.explanation: The client formally requests the offered address.

questions.question: Which UDP ports does DHCP use?
questions.explanation: Discover: 68 to 67. Offer/ACK: 67 to 68.

questions.question: Which L3 addresses does a DHCP Discover use?
questions.explanation: The client has no IP yet, so it uses the unknown-source and limited-broadcast addresses.

questions.question: Why is the DHCP Request also broadcast?
options: It tells the winning server "I accept" and tells losing servers to return their offered IPs
questions.explanation: Multiple servers may have offered addresses.

questions.question: A client requests DHCP and no server answers. The OS self-assigns:
questions.explanation: APIPA allows local-link communication only; it is not routable.

questions.question: Which devices should use static IP addresses?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure must always be found at the same address; end-user devices are transient.

questions.question: Type the Cisco command (base form) that relays DHCP broadcasts to a central server.
questions.explanation: Full form: ip helper-address 10.0.99.5, applied on the client-facing interface.

questions.question: On which interface do you configure ip helper-address?
questions.explanation: The router intercepts the client broadcast there and forwards it as a unicast.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the giaddr field?
options: It tells the remote server which subnet/pool the request came from
questions.explanation: The relay inserts its client-facing interface IP, e.g. 192.168.10.1.

questions.question: At 50% of the lease (T1) the client:
options: Unicasts a DHCP Request to its original server to renew
questions.explanation: A successful renewal resets the timer.

questions.question: At 87.5% (T2), with the original server unreachable, the client:
options: Broadcasts a DHCP Request to any server (rebinding)
Unicasts to the same server again
questions.explanation: If this fails and the lease reaches 100%, the client must surrender the IP.

questions.question: Which command must be entered before creating the DHCP pool?
questions.explanation: Exclude the gateway, switches, servers and printers first so the router never leases them.

questions.question: How does a Cisco router detect that a rogue device already uses an IP?
options: It pings the address before offering it; a reply flags a conflict
questions.explanation: Flagged addresses appear in show ip dhcp conflict.

questions.question: Type the command that shows leased IPs with the client MAC and lease expiry.
questions.explanation: show ip dhcp pool shows scope utilization instead.

questions.question: Why run DHCP on a branch router instead of only in the data center?
options: Local clients still get IPs if the WAN to the data center drops
questions.explanation: It also removes a single point of failure and reduces infrastructure.

questions.question: True or False: DORA stands for Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
questions.explanation: The client starts with no IP, so all four steps rely on Layer 2 MAC broadcasts and Layer 3 IP broadcasts until the lease is finalized.

questions.question: True or False: The client's DHCP Request in the DORA process is sent as a unicast directly to the winning server.
questions.explanation: It is broadcast. That single broadcast both tells the winning server "I accept" and tells any other servers that made offers to return those IPs to their pools.

questions.question: True or False: An APIPA address (169.254.x.x) is routable across the Internet.
questions.explanation: APIPA is a link-local fallback the OS self-assigns when no DHCP server answers. It allows only local Layer 2 communication on the same switch, never Internet routing.

questions.question: Match each DORA phase to what happens during it.
pairs: Client broadcasts, looking for any available DHCP server
A server reserves an IP from its pool and proposes it
Client broadcasts acceptance of one specific offer
Server finalizes the lease: IP, mask, gateway, duration
questions.explanation: Because the client has no IP yet, Discover and Request both travel as Layer 2 and Layer 3 broadcasts; Offer and Acknowledge come from the server on UDP port 67 to client port 68.

questions.question: Which prompt indicates Privileged EXEC mode?
questions.explanation: > is User EXEC; # is Privileged EXEC.

questions.question: Type the command to move from User EXEC to Privileged EXEC.
questions.explanation: Then configure terminal enters Global Configuration.

questions.question: Type a command that saves the running configuration to NVRAM.
questions.explanation: Run it from Privileged EXEC. RAM is volatile; a reboot wipes unsaved changes.

questions.question: Where is the startup configuration stored?
questions.explanation: The running configuration is in volatile RAM.

questions.question: What does do show ip route allow inside config-if mode?
options: Running a Privileged EXEC command without leaving the sub-mode
questions.explanation: The do override executes EXEC commands from any config mode.

questions.question: What does no shutdown do on an interface?
questions.explanation: Router interfaces are administratively down by default.

questions.question: Which sequence secures the console port?
options: line con 0, then password, then login
questions.explanation: login forces the password prompt.

questions.question: Which statement about enable secret and service password-encryption is most accurate?
options: enable secret stores a hash; service password-encryption applies only weak, reversible (Type 7) encryption to plaintext passwords
questions.explanation: Type 7 is easily reversed, so it only defeats casual shoulder-surfing.

questions.question: Packet Tracer is best described as a:
questions.explanation: It cannot reproduce obscure software bugs or hardware quirks.

questions.question: GNS3, EVE-NG and Cisco CML are:
options: Emulators that boot real Cisco IOS images
questions.explanation: They use hypervisors like QEMU to run the same binaries as physical hardware.

questions.question: What does Simulation mode in Packet Tracer let you do?
options: Pause time and inspect each PDU at every OSI layer
questions.explanation: You can watch the router strip and rewrite the L2 header while L3 IPs stay the same.

questions.question: In Packet Tracer the first ping shows "Request timed out" and the next three succeed. Why?
options: The first echo is lost while ARP resolves the destination MAC; then it is cached
questions.explanation: After the ARP reply, the MAC is cached and pings 2, 3 and 4 succeed instantly.

questions.question: Which cable connects a PC's FastEthernet port to a switch port?
questions.explanation: Different device types use straight-through cables (Auto-MDIX handles the rest on modern gear).

questions.question: True or False: Cisco Packet Tracer runs the same real IOS binaries used on physical hardware.
questions.explanation: Packet Tracer is a simulator that mimics IOS behavior from a programmed database; it is GNS3, EVE-NG, and Cisco CML that use hypervisors to boot real IOS binary images.

questions.question: Match each Cisco IOS prompt to its configuration mode.
questions.explanation: User EXEC is "look but don't touch"; Privileged EXEC is entered with enable; Global Configuration is entered with configure terminal; Interface mode is entered with interface followed by the interface name.

questions.question: Do 802.1Q VLAN tags and CoS bits survive a routed hop?
options: No: the router strips the L2 header; map CoS to DSCP in the IP header for end-to-end QoS
Yes, but only on trunk links
questions.explanation: Downstream routers read DSCP and apply local queuing priorities.

questions.question: A packet exceeds the path MTU with DF = 1. What happens?
options: The router drops it and returns ICMP Type 3, Code 4 with the next-hop MTU
The router forwards it with TTL 0
The router sends a TCP RST
questions.explanation: This is the basis of Path MTU Discovery; the source shrinks its TCP MSS.

questions.question: Why does IP use TTL and routing loop prevention?
options: Loop prevention protects the control plane; TTL is the data plane fail-safe if a loop forms anyway
TTL is used only by BGP
questions.explanation: Convergence delays or bad static routes can still create real loops.

questions.question: Dynamic ARP Inspection decides whether an ARP packet is legitimate using:
questions.explanation: A port/MAC/IP mismatch means the spoofed ARP is dropped in hardware.

questions.question: A packet is "punted" to the router's CPU when:
options: Its destination is one of the router's own interface IPs or a control-plane multicast such as OSPF 224.0.0.5
questions.explanation: Transit packets are forwarded by the ASIC using the FIB.

questions.question: A host's default gateway is set to an ordinary PC's IP on the same subnet. What happens?
options: Frames reach the PC, which drops them because IP forwarding is off: a black hole
The PC routes them to the Internet
The host falls back to APIPA
questions.explanation: The NIC accepts the frame but the OS discards the packet not addressed to itself.

questions.question: Two switches are cabled in a loop and one of them is unmanaged (no STP). What happens?
options: Broadcasts loop and multiply until buffers overflow and the CPU locks up
The frames are dropped after TTL reaches 0
questions.explanation: Layer 2 frames have no TTL. Managed switches use STP to block a port.

questions.question: How long does classic STP take to converge, compared to Rapid STP?
options: About 30 to 50 seconds vs. about 2 seconds
questions.explanation: Ports move through Blocking/Listening states before Forwarding.

questions.question: A TCP Window Size of 0 means:
options: The receiver's buffer is full; the sender halts and sends zero-window probes
The sender may send unlimited data
questions.explanation: Transmission resumes when the receiver advertises a non-zero window.

questions.question: Host A is 192.168.1.10/24 and Host B is 192.168.1.130/25 on the same switch. What is the core problem?
options: They disagree about what is on-link, so B sends its replies via its default gateway (or has none) and traffic is asymmetric
ARP cannot be broadcast with a /25
questions.explanation: ARP still works (replies are unicast to the requester); the failure is at Layer 3 return traffic.

questions.question: True or False: TTL and routing-loop-prevention protocols like AS-Path both protect the same plane: the control plane.
questions.explanation: They protect different planes. Loop-prevention mechanisms (Split Horizon, Poison Reverse, AS-Path) protect the control plane by stopping routers from building a looping map. TTL is the data-plane fail-safe: it kills a packet that is actually looping, regardless of what the control plane believes.

questions.question: True or False: A TCP Window Size of 0 tells the sender to stop transmitting until the receiver's buffer clears.
questions.explanation: The sender halts and periodically sends 1-byte Zero Window Probes; once the receiver's CPU drains its backlog, it advertises a non-zero window and transmission resumes.
